title: Built-up growth near Japanese weather stations in 1975-2020 did not explain the later animal first dates; the animal delay was larger at stations that were already built-up, mainly after 1997
abstract: Question: JMA stopped its animal phenology records in 2020 because urbanization made animals hard to find near stations. Earlier campaign work found that animal first dates became about 1.1 days per decade later than plant dates after local temperature control. Does measured built-up growth near the stations explain this delay? Data: the JMA panel of sci:71c9a88e (101 stations, 53 items, 1953-2020, GHCN-M temperature) and GHSL built-up surface (100 m; 1975, 1990, 2020) within 0.5-5 km of each station. Method: per-series temperature-adjusted trends; a pre-specified test of the animal-minus-plant interaction with 1975-2020 built-up change within 2 km (item effects, station-clustered errors); a two-way fixed-effects panel; habitat groups; regions and sub-periods. Results: built-up change did not predict the animal delay (+0.23 days/decade per +10 points, 95% CI -1.08 to 1.54; panel -0.00, CI -1.01 to 1.00), and wetland animals did not respond more than plants. Exploratory: the 1975 built-up level predicted a larger animal-minus-plant trend in 1976-2020 (+0.55, CI 0.26 to 0.85; held at all radii and within regions), but this contrast was near zero to 1996 and appeared in 1997-2008 (+0.83 days, CI 0.40 to 1.27); 58% of it came from plants that advanced more at built-up stations. At zero built-up, the 1953-2020 animal gap was still +0.91 days/decade (CI 0.35 to 1.47). Limitation: built-up surface does not measure paddy or wetland loss, search effort or station moves; the level result is exploratory.
